A linear equation has the general form:

Steps:

  1. Move variable terms to one side.

Example

3x−5=16⇒3x=21⇒x=7

Example

5x+2=3x+8⇒5x−3x=8−2⇒2x=6⇒x=3

SAT Tip: Always combine like terms before solving.

Example

x3+x6=5

Multiply through by the least common multiple (LCM) of the denominators:

6(x3+x6)=6(5)⇒2x+x=30⇒3x=30⇒x=10

    - Correct: x+5x=1+5x

Solve 3x+7=16

Balancing equations

What you do to one side, do to the other.

Solve 2(x+3)−(x−5)=12

2x+6−x+5=12⇒x+11=12⇒x=1

Fractions

  • Multiply through by least common denominator (LCD).

Example
Solve x3+25=1
Multiply both sides by 15:

5x+6=15⇒x=95

Decimals

Example

2x+5=13⇒x=4

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 8 - Systems of Equations for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

Example 1
Solve:

y=2x+3 3x+y=12

Substitute y=2x+3:

3x+(2x+3)=12⇒5x+3=12⇒5x=9⇒x=95

.
Then y=2(95)+3=185+155=335.

Solution: (95,335).

  • Add or subtract equations to eliminate one variable.

Example 2
Solve:

2x+3y=12 4x−3y=6

Add equations: 6x=18⇒x=3.
Substitute: 2(3)+3y=12⇒6+3y=12⇒y=2.
Solution: (3,2).

  • No solution (inconsistent): parallel lines with different intercepts.
    Example: y=2x+3, y=2x−4.

  • Infinite solutions (dependent): equations are multiples of each other.
    Example: 2x+4y=6, x+2y=3.

Example 3
A movie ticket costs \12foradultsand\8 for children. If 5 tickets cost \$52, how many adult and child tickets?

Let a = adults, c = children.

a+c=5 12a+8c=52

Multiply first eqn by 8: 8a+8c=40. Subtract from second: 4a=12⇒a=3.
Then c=2.

Solution: 3 adult, 2 child tickets.

Sometimes 3 equations with 3 unknowns.

Example 4
Solve:

x+y+z=6 2x−y+z=4 x+2y−z=5

From first: z=6−x−y.
Substitute into second: 2x−y+(6−x−y)=4⇒x−2y+6=4⇒x−2y=−2⇒x=2y−2.

Sub into third: (2y−2)+2y−(6−(2y−2)−y)=5.
Simplify: 2y−2+2y−(6−2y+2−y)=5.

4y−2−(8−3y)=5

.

4y−2−8+3y=5⇒7y−10=5⇒7y=15⇒y=157

.

Then x=2(157)−2=307−147=167.

z=6−167−157=42−317=117

.

Solution: (167,157,117).

  • Each equation = line.
  • Solution = intersection point(s).
  • No intersection → no solution.
  • Same line → infinite solutions.

Example 5

y=2x+1

and y=−x+4

.
Graph: they intersect at (1,3).

  • Always check the form: sometimes substitution is easier, sometimes elimination.
  • Be alert for “trick” systems (no solution or infinite).
  • Graphs can help visualize.
  • For word problems: define variables clearly, then set up equations.

1) Solve:

x+2y=7 3x−y=5

2) Solve:

2x+3y=10 4x+6y=12

3) Tickets to a play cost \5forstudentsand\12 for adults. If 10 tickets total \$81, how many of each type?

4) Solve:

x+y=4 x−y=2

5) Solve the 3-variable system:

x+2y+z=9 2x−y+z=4 x−y+2z=8

1) From first: x=7−2y. Substitute: 3(7−2y)−y=5⇒21−6y−y=5⇒−7y=−16⇒y=167. Then x=7−327=177. Solution: (177,167).

2) Second eqn is multiple of first but different constant → no solution.

3) s+a=10, 5s+12a=81. Multiply first by 5: 5s+5a=50. Subtract: 7a=31⇒a=317 (not integer). On SAT, maybe trick - check wording.

4) Add equations: 2x=6⇒x=3. Then 3+y=4⇒y=1. Solution: (3,1).

5) From first: x=9−2y−z. Substitute into second: 2(9−2y−z)−y+z=4⇒18−4y−2z−y+z=4⇒−5y−z=−14⇒5y+z=14. Call this (A).
Also substitute into third: (9−2y−z)−y+2z=8⇒9−3y+z=8⇒−3y+z=−1⇒3y−z=1. Call this (B).
Add (A)+(B): 8y=15⇒y=158. Then 3(158)−z=1⇒458−z=1⇒z=378. Then x=9−2(158)−378=72−30−378=58.
Solution: (58,158,378).

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 9 - Inequalities for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Rules are similar to solving equations, with one key difference:
- When multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign flips.

Example 1
Solve: 3x−7<11

3x<18⇒x<6

Example 2
Solve: −2x+5≥9

−2x≥4⇒x≤−2

Translate carefully from words to math.

Example 3
A concert ticket costs \40.Youhaveatmost\250. How many tickets can you buy?

40x≤250⇒x≤6.25

So maximum whole tickets = 6.

Example 4
A test requires at least 70 points to pass. You currently have 42 points out of 60. How many of the remaining 40 points must you get?

Let x = points you score on last part.

42+x≥70⇒x≥28

So you must earn at least 28 points.

  • For one-variable inequalities:
  • x<3 → open circle at 3, shade left.

  • x≥−2 → closed circle at -2, shade right.

  • For two-variable inequalities:

  • Example: y≤2x+1 → graph line y=2x+1. Shade below because of ≤.
  • Use dashed line for < or >; solid line for ≤ or ≥.

Example 5
Graph solution set of:

y>−x+2

Line: y=−x+2, slope −1, intercept 2. Dashed line. Shade region above.

The solution is the overlap region of all shaded areas.

Example 6
Graph and solve:

y≥x+1 y<−2x+4

The solution region is the intersection of the two shaded half-planes.

  • Always flip the inequality when multiplying/dividing by negative.

content:
A percent is a ratio out of 100.

Percent=PartWhole×100
  • 50% = 50100=12
  • 25% = 25100=14

Formula

Percent Change=New−OriginalOriginal×100%
  • Positive → increase
  • Negative → decrease

Examples
1. Price from \40to\50:

50−4040×100=25% increase
  1. Price from \80to\60:
60−8080×100=−25% decrease

Simple Interest

I=Prt
  • P = principal

  • t = time

Example: \1000at5I = 1000(0.05)(3)=150$

Compound Interest

A=P(1+rn)nt
  • A = total
  • P = principal
  • r = annual rate (decimal)
  • n = times compounded per year
  • t = time in years

Example: \$1000 at 5% compounded annually for 3 years

0.40×200=80

Example 2

- After discount: 100(0.8)=80
- After tax: 80(1.05)=84

  • Linear growth: constant addition per step
    Example: salary increases \2000eachyear→y=2000t+P$
  • Exponential growth: constant multiplication per step

y=y0+kt
  • k>0: growth

Example

y=200−5t

y=y0(1±r)t
  • + for growth

  • Positive association: as x increases, y tends to increase.
  • Negative association: as x increases, y tends to decrease.

A unit rate expresses the rate per 1 unit.

Examples - 180 miles in 3 hours → 1803=60 miles/hour
- \12for4poundsofapples→\dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ dollars/pound

A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, used to change units.

Common examples - 1 hour=60 minutes
- 1 inch=2.54 cm
- 1 mile=5280 ft

Example
Convert 5 hours to minutes:

5 hr·60 min1 hr=300 min

  • d=rt

r=1803=60 mph

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 10 - Word Problems for SAT Math preparation.
content:
Example 1
A number increased by 7 is 20. Find the number.

Let x = the number.

x+7=20⇒x=13

Example 2
A rectangle has length 3 more than twice its width. If the perimeter is 42, find dimensions.

Let width = w, length = 2w+3.

2w+2(2w+3)=42⇒2w+4w+6=42⇒6w=36⇒w=6

Then l=2(6)+3=15.
Rectangle: 6×15.

Distance = rate × time.

Example 3
A car travels 60 miles in the same time a train travels 100 miles. If the train is twice as fast, find car’s speed.

Let r = car speed. Train speed = 2r.
Time = distance/rate.

60r=1002r⇒60r=50r

Contradiction → no solution. Check: maybe train is not exactly twice but “20 mph faster.”

Revised Problem
Car: r, Train: r+20, Times equal.

60r=100r+20

Cross-multiply: 60(r+20)=100r⇒60r+1200=100r⇒40r=1200⇒r=30.
Car = 30 mph, Train = 50 mph.

Work rate = 1 / (time to finish).

Example 4
Alice can paint a room in 4 hours, Bob in 6 hours. How long together?

Rates: Alice = 1/4, Bob = 1/6. Together = 1/4+1/6=5/12.
So time = 1/(5/12)=12/5=2.4 hours.

Example 5
A 20-liter solution is 25% acid. How much water to add to make it 10% acid?

Acid = 0.25(20)=5 liters.
Final solution: 20+x liters, still 5 acid.

520+x=0.10⇒5=0.1(20+x)⇒5=2+0.1x⇒0.1x=3⇒x=30

Add 30 liters water.

Example 6
Find three consecutive integers whose sum is 96.

Let numbers = n,n+1,n+2.

n+(n+1)+(n+2)=96⇒3n+3=96⇒3n=93⇒n=31

Numbers: 31, 32, 33.

  • Define variables before writing equations.
  • Watch out for “at least,” “at most” (inequalities).
  • Always answer in the context of the problem (no raw variables).
  • Plug answer choices back in if stuck (backsolving).

Try: 600/(r+300)=200/r. Cross multiply: 600r=200(r+300)⇒600r=200r+60,000⇒400r=60,000⇒r=150. Car = 150 mph, Plane = 450 mph.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 12 - Interpreting Linear Models for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Slope is the change in y per unit change in x.
  • Interpreted as a rate.

Example 1
A taxi company charges according to the equation:

Cost=2.5x+4

where x = miles traveled.

  • Slope = 2.5 → cost increases by \$2.50 per mile.
  • Intercept = 4 → flat starting fee = \$4.
  • Intercept is the value of y when x=0.
  • Often represents initial condition.

Example 2
Temperature T=70−2t, where t = hours after noon.

  • Intercept = 70 → temperature at noon = 70°F.
  • Slope = -2 → temperature drops 2°F each hour.

You can use the equation to predict values.

Example 3
A company’s revenue is modeled by:

R=5000+200t

where t = months.

  • After 6 months:
R=5000+200(6)=6200

So revenue = \$6200.

  • Models may not apply for all x.
  • Negative values may be meaningless (e.g., negative time, negative price).
  • Always check context.

Example 4
If h=100−5t gives height of rocket (t= seconds), then at t=30:

h=100−150=−50

Negative height is meaningless → model only valid for small t.

On the SAT:
- A line of best fit is given.
- You may be asked to interpret slope/intercept.
- Or check if a point fits the model.

Example 5
Scatterplot shows relation between study hours (x) and test score (y). Line of best fit:

y=50+5x
  • Intercept = 50 → baseline score with 0 study = 50.
  • Slope = 5 → each study hour adds 5 points.
  • Identify units for slope/intercept.
  • Watch for unrealistic predictions.
  • If a graph/table is shown, pick two points to compute slope.
  • Double-check whether the model describes growth or decline.

4) The line of best fit for data is y=30+4x. Interpret slope in context.

2) Slope = -1200 → car loses \$1200 value each year.

3) W=180−2(5)=170. After 5 weeks, weight = 170 lbs.

4) Slope = 4 → each increase of 1 unit in x raises y by 4.

content:

  • Mode: The most frequent value.

Example 1
Data: [2,3,3,4,5]
- Mean =(2+3+3+4+5)/5=17/5=3.4
- Median =3
- Mode =3

  • Range:
Range=Max−Min
  • Standard Deviation (SD):
    A measure of how spread out data is.
    Larger SD → more spread.
    Smaller SD → values closer to the mean.

Example 2
Set A: [10,10,10,10] → SD = 0 (no spread).
Set B: [5,10,15] → larger spread, larger SD.

  • Histogram: Shows frequency of values in intervals (bins).
  • Dot Plot: Uses dots above a number line to show frequency.

SAT often asks:
- Which interval is most common?
- Approximate median/mean from the graph.

Example 3
The average of 4 test scores is 80. If three of them are 85, 75, 90, find the missing score.

85+75+90+x4=80⇒250+x=320⇒x=70
  • Always sort data before finding the median.
  • If one value is much larger/smaller → mean shifts, median less affected.
  • SD questions are usually relative (“which set has greater spread?”).
  • Carefully read graph axes.

1) Find the mean of [4,6,8,10].
2) Data: [2,5,7,8,12]. What is the median?
3) What is the mode of [1,2,2,3,4,4,4,5]?
4) Find the range of [9,14,22,5,17].
5) A histogram shows most students scored between 70–80. What does this tell you about the mode?

1) Mean =(4+6+8+10)/4=28/4=7.

2) Ordered set [2,5,7,8,12] → median =7.

3) Mode =4 (appears 3 times).

4) Range =22−5=17.

5) The mode is in the 70–80 interval.

related_skills: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 25 - Statistics II for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Random Sample: Every member has equal chance of being selected → most reliable.
  • Biased Sample: Favors certain members → unreliable.

Example
Surveying only basketball players to estimate average student height = biased.
Surveying random students across school = better.

Scatterplots often include a regression line.

  • Positive slope: As x increases, y tends to increase.
  • Negative slope: As x increases, y tends to decrease.
  • Closer points to line: Stronger correlation.

Example
If best-fit line is y^=2x+5, then for x=4:

y^=2(4)+5=13

Every estimate from a sample has some uncertainty.

  • Smaller sample size → larger margin of error.
  • Larger sample size → smaller margin of error.

Example
Poll shows 60% ± 3%. True population proportion is likely between 57% and 63%.

A confidence interval provides a range that likely contains the true population value.

  • A 95% confidence interval means if the survey were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true value.

Example
A survey estimates average GPA = 3.2 with 95% CI (3.0,3.4).
Interpretation: The true GPA is likely between 3.0 and 3.4.

  • Correlation does not imply causation!
  • Randomized controlled experiments are most reliable.
  • Observational studies can show association but not cause.

Example
Data shows students who eat breakfast score higher.
Conclusion: Eating breakfast is associated with higher scores, but may not be the cause (other factors like sleep could matter).

  • Look for wording like biased, random, representative.
  • Be careful: SAT may trick with causation vs. correlation.
  • For line of best fit → always use the equation given, not your own guess.
  • Interpret margin of error and confidence intervals correctly.

1) A school surveys only students in the honor society to estimate average study time. Is this sample biased?

2) A scatterplot shows a strong negative correlation. What does this mean?

3) A poll shows 48% support ± 4%. What is the interval of possible true support?

4) A best-fit line is y^=−3x+20. Predict y^ when x=5.

5) Researchers observe that students who text more tend to sleep less. Can they conclude texting causes less sleep?

1) Yes - it’s biased, since only honor students are surveyed.

2) As x increases, y tends to decrease.

3) Interval = (44%,52%).

4) y^=−3(5)+20=−15+20=5.

5) No - it only shows correlation, not causation.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 11 - Lines for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Slope (m): measures steepness.
m=riserun=y2−y1x2−x1
  • y-intercept (b): point where line crosses y-axis.

Equation form:

y=mx+b

Example 1
Find slope and intercept of line through (2,3) and (4,7).

m=7−34−2=42=2

Equation: y=2x+b. Plug (2,3): 3=2(2)+b⇒3=4+b⇒b=−1.
Final: y=2x−1.

Slope-Intercept Form

y=mx+b

Point-Slope Form

y−y1=m(x−x1)

Example 2
Equation of line through (1,2) with slope −3:

y−2=−3(x−1)⇒y=−3x+5

Solve system of equations.

Example 3
Find intersection of y=2x+1 and y=−x+4.

Set equal:

2x+1=−x+4⇒3x=3⇒x=1

Then y=2(1)+1=3.
Intersection = (1,3).

  • Parallel lines: same slope, different intercepts.
  • Perpendicular lines: slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).

Example 4
Find equation of line parallel to y=3x+2 through (0,5).

Slope = 3. Equation: y=3x+5.

Example 5
Find equation of line perpendicular to y=12x−1 through (2,0).

Slope = −1(12)=−2.
Equation: y−0=−2(x−2)⇒y=−2x+4.

  • Horizontal: y=c (slope = 0).
  • Vertical: x=c (slope undefined).

Example 6
Equation of line through (3,−2) and parallel to y=−2:
Answer: y=−2.

Example 7
Equation of line through (4,5) and parallel to x=1:
Answer: x=4.

  • Memorize slope formulas.
  • Parallel → same m.
  • Perpendicular → m1·m2=−1.
  • Watch out for vertical/horizontal lines.
  • For intersections, substitution is often faster than graphing.

1) Find slope and intercept of line through (0,4) and (2,10).
2) Write equation of line with slope 5 through (1,−3).
3) Find intersection of y=3x+1 and y=−2x+6.
4) Write equation of line parallel to y=−4x+7 through (2,1).
5) Write equation of line perpendicular to y=2x−5 through (−1,2).

1) m=(10−4)/(2−0)=6/2=3. Equation: y=3x+4.

2) Point-slope: y+3=5(x−1)⇒y=5x−8.

3) 3x+1=−2x+6⇒5x=5⇒x=1,y=4. Intersection (1,4).

4) Parallel slope −4. Equation: y−1=−4(x−2)⇒y=−4x+9.

5) Perpendicular slope −12. Equation: y−2=−12(x+1)⇒y=−12x+32.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 18 - Angles for SAT Math preparation.
content:
In a triangle, the exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

Exterior Angle=Remote Interior Angle 1+Remote Interior Angle 2

Example 1
In a triangle, one exterior angle is 120∘. If one remote interior angle is 40∘, the other is:

120∘−40∘=80∘

When a transversal cuts two parallel lines:

  • Corresponding angles are equal.
  • Alternate interior angles are equal.
  • Same-side interior angles are supplementary.

Example 2
If one angle is 70∘, then the corresponding angle is also 70∘.

Interior Angle Sum

For an n-sided polygon:

Sum of interior angles=(n−2)×180∘

Each Interior Angle (regular polygon)

(n−2)×180∘n

Each Exterior Angle (regular polygon)

360∘n

Example 3
A hexagon (n=6):
- Interior angle sum =(6−2)×180=720∘
- Each interior angle =720/6=120∘

  • Complementary angles: sum =90∘
  • Supplementary angles: sum =180∘
  • Vertical angles: equal

Example 4
If two supplementary angles are in ratio 2:7, find them.

2x+7x=180⇒9x=180⇒x=20

Angles = 40∘,140∘

  • Always check for parallel lines → look for equal angles.
  • For polygons, memorize (n−2)×180∘.
  • Exterior angle theorem is very common.
  • Watch out for “trick” wording with supplements/complements.

1) In a triangle, one angle is 50∘ and another is 60∘. Find the exterior angle adjacent to the third angle.
2) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If one angle is 75∘, find its alternate interior angle.
3) Find the sum of interior angles of a decagon.
4) Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.
5) Two angles are complementary. One is x, the other is 2x. Solve for x.

1) Third angle =180−50−60=70∘. Exterior angle = 180−70=110∘.

2) Alternate interior angle = 75∘.

3) (10−2)×180=8×180=1440∘.

4) (8−2)×180/8=6×180/8=108∘.

5) x+2x=90⇒3x=90⇒x=30.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 19 - Triangles for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Isosceles Triangle: 2 equal sides → 2 equal angles.
  • Equilateral Triangle: All sides equal, all angles =60∘.

Example 1
If an isosceles triangle has vertex angle 40∘, each base angle is:

180−402=70∘

A right triangle has one 90∘ angle.
Pythagorean theorem:

a2+b2=c2

where c is the hypotenuse.

Common triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25), (8,15,17).

45-45-90 Triangle

  • Legs equal.
  • Hypotenuse =leg·2.

30-60-90 Triangle

  • Short leg =x.
  • Hypotenuse =2x.
  • Long leg =x3.

Example 2
In a 30-60-90 triangle, if the hypotenuse is 10, then:
- Short leg =5
- Long leg =53

Triangles are similar if their angles are equal and sides proportional.

a1a2=b1b2=c1c2

Example 3
If △ABC~△DEF, and AB=4, BC=6, EF=9, find DE.

Scale factor =69=23.
So DE=AB·32=4·32=6.

Radians measure angles in terms of arc length.

180∘=π radians

Conversions:
- Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
- Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

Example 4
Convert 120∘ to radians:

120∘·π180=2π3
  • Always check if triangle is special (30-60-90 or 45-45-90).
  • Use Pythagorean triples to save time.
  • Mark equal sides/angles in isosceles problems.
  • Watch for hidden similar triangles (especially in geometry diagrams).

1) Find the missing angle in a triangle with angles 40∘ and 75∘.
2) In an isosceles triangle, the vertex angle is 100∘. Find the base angles.
3) A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse.
4) In a 45-45-90 triangle, the hypotenuse is 8. Find the legs.
5) Convert 225∘ into radians.
6) Two similar triangles have sides 3,4,5 and 6,x,10. Find x.

1) 180−40−75=65∘.

2) Base angles =(180−100)/2=40∘.

3) c=92+122=81+144=225=15.

4) Leg =8/2=42.

5) 225∘·π/180=5π4.

6) Scale factor =2. So x=8.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 20 - Circles for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Circumference:
C=2πr=πd
  • Area:
A=πr2

Example 1
If r=7, then:

C=14π,A=49π

Arc length is a portion of the circumference:

s=θ360∘·2πr

(or s=θr if θ in radians).

Example 2
Find the arc length of a 90∘ arc in a circle of radius 4.

s=90360·2π(4)=2π

Sector area is a portion of the total area:

Asector=θ360∘·πr2

(or Asector=12r2θ if θ in radians).

Example 3
Find the area of a 60∘ sector with r=6:

A=60360·π(36)=6π
  • Central angle: vertex at the circle’s center, equals arc measure.
  • Inscribed angle: vertex on the circle, equals half the arc it intercepts.

Example 4
If arc AB=80∘, then:
- Central angle =80∘
- Inscribed angle =40∘

General form:

(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2

where (h,k) is the center and r the radius.

Example 5
Equation of circle centered at (3,−2) with r=5:

(x−3)2+(y+2)2=25
  • Inscribed angle = half arc is very common.
  • For arc/sector problems, always check if θ is in degrees or radians.
  • If you see x2+y2 terms, think “equation of a circle.”
  • Don’t forget diameter =2r when needed.

1) Find the circumference of a circle with r=10.
2) Find the area of a circle with diameter 12.
3) In a circle of radius 5, find the length of an arc subtended by 72∘.
4) Find the area of a 90∘ sector with r=8.
5) In a circle, arc AB=100∘. Find the inscribed angle subtending that arc.
6) Write the equation of a circle centered at (2,3) with radius 7.

1) C=2π(10)=20π.

2) r=6⇒A=π(36)=36π.

3) s=72360·2π(5)=2π.

4) A=90360·π(64)=16π.

5) Inscribed angle =100/2=50∘.

6) (x−2)2+(y−3)2=49.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 21 - Trigonometry for SAT Math preparation.
content:
In a right triangle:

sinθ=oppositehypotenuse,cosθ=adjacenthypotenuse,tanθ=oppositeadjacent

Example 1
In a right triangle, opposite =3, adjacent =4, hypotenuse =5:

sinθ=35,cosθ=45,tanθ=34

Pythagorean Identity

sin2θ+cos2θ=1

Tangent Identity

tanθ=sinθcosθ,cosθ≠0

Example 2
If sinθ=513, find cosθ.

cosθ=1−sin2θ=1−25169=1213
  • Use special right triangles (30-60-90, 45-45-90).

sin30∘=12,cos30∘=32,tan30∘=13 sin45∘=22,cos45∘=22,tan45∘=1 sin60∘=32,cos60∘=12,tan60∘=3

Example 3
Evaluate tan45∘:

tan45∘=1
  • Draw the reference triangle if possible.
  • Memorize exact values for 30∘,45∘,60∘.
  • Use sin2+cos2=1 to find missing values.
  • Watch for trick questions mixing degrees and radians.

1) In a right triangle, opposite =8, hypotenuse =17. Find sinθ and cosθ.
2) If cosθ=1213, find sinθ.
3) Evaluate sin30∘+cos60∘.
4) Find tanθ if sinθ=513 and cosθ=1213.
5) Simplify sin245∘+cos245∘.

1) Adjacent =172−82=289−64=225=15.

sinθ=817,cosθ=1517

3) sin30∘=12, cos60∘=12 → sum =1.

description: Comprehensive lesson covering Unit 26 - Volume for SAT Math preparation.
content:
• Prism (rectangular box, etc.):
V=Base Area×Height
  • Cylinder:
V=πr2h

Example 1
A cylinder has radius 3 and height 10.

V=π(32)(10)=90π
  • Pyramid:
V=13(Base Area)(Height)
  • Cone:
V=13πr2h

Example 2
A cone with radius 4 and height 9:

V=13π(42)(9)=48π
V=43πr3

Example 3
A sphere with radius 5:

V=43π(53)=5003π

Sometimes shapes are combined or parts are removed.
Strategy: Add or subtract volumes.

Example 4
A cylinder with r=3,h=10 is filled with a cone (r=3,h=10).
Volume difference = πr2h−13πr2h=23πr2h

=23π(9)(10)=60π
  • Always confirm if radius or diameter is given.
  • Watch units! SAT may ask in cubic centimeters, etc.
  • If asked about volume change, compare ratios instead of recalculating everything.
  • Example: If radius doubles, sphere’s volume increases by factor 23=8.

1) Find the volume of a rectangular box with dimensions 4×5×6.

2) A sphere has radius 7. Find its volume.

3) A cone has diameter 10 and height 12. Find its volume.

4) A cylinder has radius 5 and height 20. Find its volume.

5) If the radius of a sphere doubles, by what factor does its volume increase?

1) V=4×5×6=120.

2) V=43π(73)=13723π.

3) Radius = 5.

V=13π(52)(12)=100π

4) V=π(52)(20)=500π.

5) Volume increases by 23=8 times.
